title: Tool calls own preparation, dispatch, and results by callId
summary: A tool call is shown in three stages keyed by its call id: 'preparing' as soon as the model streams a tool name, 'start' when the complete call arrives, 'result' when the result arrives. The preparing stage is display only and changes no session event and no dispatch timing.
firstReason: Without it the UI shows no activity for the seconds a model spends streaming a long argument such as file content. The three-stage model moves into the Go host's view of the conversation and is pushed to the page over server-sent events.

title: Domain image Slots and a shared gallery Factory
summary: User messages, assistant output, trajectory records and tool results each declare their own image slot, and the attachment plugin fills all four with one shared gallery component.
firstReason: Slots and factories are the React client's extension mechanism. Server-rendered HTML gets the same reuse from one gallery template partial called from four places; whether third parties can replace it depends on the UI extension model the Go design adopts.

title: Standard reasoning Body Slot and reusable Content Factory
summary: The reasoning body is a named slot that plugins can replace or wrap, and the standard Markdown rendering of reasoning is a separately registered factory that replacements can call.
firstReason: It separates 'where content goes' from 'the default way to draw it', so that a wrapper such as translation reuses the default. In Go templates the same split is a named block plus a reusable partial; the registration machinery is React-specific.

title: Chat group-tree positions and exchanges
summary: A turn started by a notice (a finished subagent, a schedule, a background job) is not a new user message: it does not fold the previous turn. The 'latest' part of the chat is the latest exchange, defined by typed positions of nodes in a group tree.
firstReason: The visible rule (notices do not collapse what the reader is looking at) should be kept. The group-tree typing lives in the client's node model; the Go host computes exchanges when it renders the conversation.

title: One fold motion for collapsing on the next message
summary: Collapsing the previous exchange when the next message arrives uses one animation path that moves row heights and scroll position together, in batches.
firstReason: Two fold paths produced a visible jump. The goal (no jump when earlier work collapses) stands; frame-by-frame scroll driving is client JavaScript. Inference: the Go UI should first try native collapse with CSS scroll anchoring and add script only if that is not enough.

title: Precompute the steering batch start in Conversation Node Definition state
summary: Whether a steering message starts a new batch after the running turn's output is computed once in conversation-node state by the node definitions, instead of being worked out at render time.
firstReason: It exists to keep a reserved 44px slot stable in the React chat. A server-side view model computes this fact when it builds the conversation; the definition-state mechanism does not carry.

title: File drag ownership outside the application layout
summary: Dragging files and images is owned by one client plugin that keeps the original files alive during a drag and shows failures in a shell overlay, so the application layout has no image-specific provider.
firstReason: The ownership problem (feature state hidden in a React ancestor) does not arise without a component tree. Browser drag and drop stays a small script island, and the rule that the original file survives its source closing still applies to it.

title: Dispatch Markdown fences by language through a keyed hoc slot
summary: Chat hands each Markdown fenced code block to a delegate, which dispatches it by language through a keyed `hoc` slot, so a plugin can register, replace or decorate the rendering of one language.
firstReason: Per-language fence rendering by extensions stays a requirement (diagrams, charts, previews). In the Go UI the Markdown renderer runs on the host, so the extension point is a host-side registry of fence renderers keyed by language, not a React slot.

title: Keep Every Assistant Reply When a Turn Folds
summary: When a finished turn folds, every assistant reply stays visible and only the process (tool calls, reasoning) folds. A general setting, `ui-chat.foldedReplies`, can restore the old rule of showing only the final answer.
firstReason: It is a reading rule about what a user must not lose, independent of the rendering technology. The host template applies it and the setting stays in host settings; DH-ADR-3 changes only where it is rendered.

title: Linear credential matching and performance gates for user text
summary: Credentials in user text shown in the UI are found with a scan that is linear in the text length: one literal-only search finds where a known credential format starts, and only then is the format checked. Performance gates keep text without credentials nearly free and hostile input linear.
firstReason: Masking credentials in displayed user text stays a requirement, but it moves to the Go host that renders the HTML (DH-ADR-3). Inference: Go's standard `regexp` package guarantees linear-time matching, so most of the hand-built protection against backtracking is unnecessary; the list of credential formats and the performance gate are what carry over.

title: Chat history prefetch and safe consumption
summary: Proposal: older chat history is fetched ahead of need but shown only at a safe moment. The client holds at most one fetched page, and the chat view decides when to insert it, so a page that arrives during a touch drag or an animation does not make the transcript jump.
firstReason: Adopt the behaviour: fetch earlier history before the reader reaches the top, and never move what they are reading. The mechanism changes because the page is an HTML fragment fetched from the Go host (DH-ADR-3); a small script island must hold the fragment and insert it with the reading position preserved.
